title: High-Profile Exits at Justice Department as Prosecutor Overseeing Trump 'Grand Conspiracy' Probe Steps Down
snippet: A post-midterm exodus at the Department of Justice continues as Miami U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones and National Security Chief John Eisenberg announce their resignations.
content:
WASHINGTON — The Justice Department is facing a major wave of high-profile departures in the wake of the midterm elections, capped Friday by the resignation of the top federal prosecutor in Miami who was overseeing a politically charged probe into opponents of President Donald Trump.

Jason Reding Quiñones, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, stepped down following growing frustration among senior Washington officials regarding his management of the so-called "grand conspiracy" investigation, according to sources familiar with the personnel moves who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

A Stalled Investigation

The Southern District of Florida had been the epicenter of a long-running, meandering inquiry examining whether former intelligence and federal law enforcement officials conspired against Trump. However, the probe has faltered in recent months due to high staff turnover and mounting delays. Federal investigators recently postponed scheduled grand jury testimony from multiple key witnesses, pointing to deep trouble within the case.

The investigation has seen multiple leadership changes over the past year. Last spring, a senior national security prosecutor was removed from the team investigating former CIA Director John Brennan after challenging the strength of the evidence. Attorney Joseph diGenova later took charge of the inquiry before abruptly resigning in September without filing any criminal charges.

Department Leadership Applauds Contributions

Despite the internal friction over the conspiracy probe, Attorney General Todd Blanche publicly praised Quiñones on social media, highlighting his efforts against violent crime, drug trafficking, and international criminal organizations—specifically pointing to his office's May indictment of former Cuban President Raúl Castro related to the 1996 shootdown of civilian aircraft.

In a farewell statement, Quiñones expressed "immense pride in what we accomplished together" and extended gratitude to Trump and his colleagues for their "unwavering commitment to justice and the rule of law."

Broader Shakeup at Main Justice

Quiñones' exit is part of a broader leadership reshuffle. Attorney General Blanche confirmed Friday that John Eisenberg, the head of the department's National Security Division, has also resigned. Sworn in during June 2025, Eisenberg managed counterterrorism, espionage, and cybercrime cases, including the high-profile prosecution of former national security adviser John Bolton, who pleaded guilty earlier this year to mishandling classified documents.

Eisenberg's departure follows Thursday's resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who spent her tenure executing a sweeping overhaul of the Civil Rights Division.
